USA-1828: During the 1820s, most states removed the property qualifications for voting, through constitutional revisions and ordinary legislation. Mass parties formed around the presidential election of 1828, in which Andrew Jackson's Democratic coalition defeated the incumbent, John Quincy Adams. No ruler was removed: power changed hands at the ballot box, within a functioning constitutional republic. The result was a legislature answerable to a much larger electorate.
DNK-1848: On 21 March 1848, after the Casino meeting, some 15,000 citizens of Copenhagen marched to Christiansborg to demand a new ministry and a free constitution. King Frederick VII declared that he had already dismissed the old ministry and that he now regarded himself as a constitutional monarch. A Constituent Assembly was elected in October 1848, and the June Constitution of 1849 created an elected parliament with legislative and budgetary powers. Absolutism ended without a single death, and the King kept his throne.
CAN-1874: In 1873 the opposition exposed the Pacific Scandal, in which Conservative campaign funds had been tied to the Canadian Pacific Railway contract. Facing defeat in Parliament, Macdonald's government resigned in November 1873, and the Liberals under Mackenzie won the election of January 1874. The new government introduced the secret ballot with the Dominion Elections Act and a law on controverted elections. The episode established that a government that loses the confidence of the House must go, and that elections are policed by the courts rather than by the executive.
FRA-1875: After the fall of the Second Empire in 1870, a monarchist National Assembly governed France without settling its regime. The Constitutional Laws of 1875, passed after the Wallon amendment, founded the Third Republic with ministers responsible to an elected Chamber of Deputies. In the crisis of 16 May 1877, President MacMahon dismissed the government and dissolved the Chamber, but the republicans won the October elections and MacMahon gave way. From then on, the executive answered to parliament.
GRC-1875: In June 1874, Charilaos Trikoupis published a newspaper article, "Who is to blame?", accusing King George I of appointing governments that lacked a parliamentary majority. He was briefly jailed. One year later, the King appointed him prime minister and, in the speech from the throne of August 1875, accepted the dedilomeni principle: he would appoint as prime minister only the leader enjoying the declared confidence of parliament. The King conceded the principle without a social uprising, and clean elections followed the same year.
NOR-1885: After the Liberal landslide in the 1882 election, the Storting impeached the King's cabinet, and the Riksrett convicted the ministers in early 1884. Rather than resist parliament, King Oscar II appointed the leader of the parliamentary majority, Johan Sverdrup, as prime minister in June 1884. This established the principle that the government must have the confidence of the Storting. The King kept his throne, and no force was used.
MEX-1911: Porfirio Díaz claimed victory in the fraudulent election of 1910, and Francisco Madero's Plan of San Luis Potosí called for an armed uprising. After the rebels took Ciudad Juárez in May 1911, Díaz resigned and went into exile, ending more than three decades of rule. Madero was elected president in October 1911. The opening was short-lived in form, as Madero was overthrown and killed in 1913, but the Porfirian system of personal rule did not return.
MEX-1997: The electoral reforms of 1994 and 1996, negotiated among the parties after the Chiapas uprising and the Colosio assassination, made the Federal Electoral Institute autonomous. In the midterm elections of July 1997, the PRI, in power since 1929, lost its majority in the Chamber of Deputies for the first time. The presidency was now faced with a legislature it did not control. In 2000, Vicente Fox won the presidency and ended 71 years of PRI rule.
ZMB-1926: Northern Rhodesia passed from the rule of the British South Africa Company to the Colonial Office in April 1924, under a Governor and a Legislative Council. The Legislative Council Ordinance of 1925 provided for elected members, and the first elections were held in May 1926. The franchise was confined to the white settler population. Still, a chartered company's administration was replaced by a legislature with an elected component.
ZMB-1991: Food riots in June 1990 and a failed coup attempt a few weeks later put Kenneth Kaunda's one-party regime under pressure. Kaunda agreed to multiparty politics, which was legalized in December 1990, and a new constitution followed in 1991. In the elections of October 1991, Frederick Chiluba's MMD won by a landslide. Kaunda handed over power peacefully, ending 27 years of UNIP rule.
IRL-1927: Fianna Fáil, founded by de Valera in 1926, had rejected the institutions of the Free State after the civil war. After the assassination of Kevin O'Higgins in July 1927, the Cosgrave government required all candidates to pledge to take their seats. Fianna Fáil took the oath and entered the Dáil in August 1927. The main opposition thereby accepted parliamentary government, and the Free State acquired a working two-party system.
GTM-1941: In June 1944, students, teachers and workers led protests and a general strike against the dictatorship of Jorge Ubico. After troops fired on a demonstration, Ubico resigned on 1 July. His successor, General Ponce Vaides, was overthrown in October 1944 by an armed uprising led by Árbenz and Arana. The junta held elections, which Arévalo won, and the Constitution of 1945 restored elections and limits on the executive.
URY-1943: Gabriel Terra's self-coup of 1933 had opened an authoritarian period. In February 1942, President Baldomir dissolved parliament and the Electoral Court in what became known as the "good coup", with the support of Batllistas and Independent Nationalists. A Council of State drafted the Constitution of 1942, which voters approved in a plebiscite held alongside the general elections of November 1942. Juan José de Amézaga took office in March 1943, and full constitutional government was restored.
BRA-1946: Pressure on Getúlio Vargas's Estado Novo grew from 1943: the Manifesto dos Mineiros, student protests, an amnesty, and a new electoral law. On 29 October 1945, the army deposed Vargas without bloodshed. Elections were held in December 1945, and the Constitution of 1946 restored an elected Congress. The dictatorship ended by a coup, but the coup handed power to an elected legislature.
BRA-1985: The opposition gained ground in the elections of 1982, and the Diretas Já campaign of 1983–84 drew crowds of up to 1.5 million, though Congress rejected direct presidential elections. In January 1985, the electoral college chose Tancredo Neves of the opposition PMDB, backed by defectors from the regime. José Sarney took office in March 1985, ending 21 years of military rule. A Constituent Assembly then wrote the Constitution of 1988.
ITA-1946: Mussolini was deposed by the Grand Council and the King in July 1943, and the armistice of September 1943 was followed by German occupation and civil war until May 1945. On 2 June 1946, a referendum abolished the monarchy and elected a Constituent Assembly. The republican Constitution took effect on 1 January 1948, founding a parliamentary republic. The old ruler was replaced, and the executive was made responsible to an elected parliament.
PHL-1946: The Commonwealth government was restored in February 1945, after the liberation from Japanese occupation, and elections were held in April 1946. On 4 July 1946, the United States granted independence on the date set by the Tydings-McDuffie Act of 1934. The new republic kept an elected Congress and president under the Constitution of 1935. The colonial power left by agreement, though the exclusion of the Democratic Alliance congressmen soon fed the Huk rebellion.
PHL-1988: The fraudulent snap election of February 1986 was followed by a military mutiny and by the People Power Revolution on EDSA, which drew millions into the streets. Ferdinand Marcos fled into exile on 25 February 1986. Corazon Aquino ruled by decree until the Constitution of 1987, ratified in February, restored an elected Congress, which sat from July 1987. The new order survived several coup attempts by the military.
JPN-1947: Japan surrendered in August 1945 and was occupied by the Allies. The postwar Constitution, drafted under the occupation in 1946 and in force from 3 May 1947, vested sovereignty in the people, reduced the emperor to a symbol of the state, and made the cabinet responsible to the Diet. The emperor kept his position. The constraints on the executive were imposed from outside, but they held once the occupation ended.
NLD-1947: The German occupation of 1940–45 ended with the surrender of May 1945. Queen Wilhelmina and the government-in-exile returned, a provisional cabinet took office, and parliamentary elections in May 1946 restored normal constitutional government. The constitutional monarchy and the elected States General resumed their prewar roles. The break in the index reflects the restoration of parliament after five years of occupation.
ECU-1948: Velasco Ibarra's self-coup of 1946 was followed by a short cycle of military interventions in 1947, after which Congress installed a civilian president. Galo Plaza won the election of June 1948, the first supervised by the Supreme Electoral Tribunal, and took office in September. His election opened twelve years of constitutional government in which three elected presidents completed their terms. This was the longest period of uninterrupted constitutional rule in Ecuador's history up to that point.
CRI-1950: In March 1948, the Congress controlled by the Calderonistas annulled Otilio Ulate's electoral victory. José Figueres's National Liberation Army rose in revolt and toppled the government after six weeks of civil war. The junta abolished the army in December 1948, had a constituent assembly adopt the Constitution of 1949, and handed power to Ulate in November 1949. The Constitution restored elected government and created an independent Supreme Electoral Tribunal.
IND-1950: Britain transferred power under the Indian Independence Act on 15 August 1947, amid the partition from Pakistan and the communal violence that accompanied it. The Constituent Assembly's Constitution took effect on 26 January 1950, establishing a parliamentary republic with universal suffrage. The first general elections followed in 1951–52. The colonial executive was replaced by a cabinet responsible to an elected Lok Sabha.
SGP-1955: Under British rule, the Rendel Commission of 1953–54 recommended a mostly elected Legislative Assembly. Elections were held in April 1955 for 25 of the 32 seats, and David Marshall's Labour Front formed the government. The colonial power conceded a legislature with an elected majority while keeping control of defence and external affairs. Internal self-government followed in 1959.
ARG-1958: The military overthrew Juan Perón in September 1955 after a failed coup attempt in June had bombed the Plaza de Mayo. The Aramburu junta put down a Peronist rising in 1956 and then held elections in February 1958. Arturo Frondizi won and took office in May 1958. The military handed power to an elected president and Congress, though with Peronism proscribed.
PER-1958: The Arequipa uprising of December 1955, a general strike and protests, forced the resignation of Manuel Odría's head of repression. A garrison revolt in February 1956 demanded free elections. Odría held elections in June 1956, which Manuel Prado won, and Prado took office in July 1956 under restored constitutional rule. The dictator left office by election rather than by force.
PER-2002: After the fraudulent re-election of 2000, mass protests and the Vladivideo scandal brought down Alberto Fujimori's regime. Fujimori fled to Japan and resigned by fax, and in November 2000 Congress removed him for "moral incapacity". Valentín Paniagua's interim government held free elections in 2001, won by Alejandro Toledo. Congress regained the powers it had lost after the self-coup of 1992.
COL-1959: The leaders of the Liberal and Conservative parties signed the pacts of Benidorm and Sitges in 1956–57 to end the dictatorship of Gustavo Rojas Pinilla. Student protests and a general strike in May 1957 led the military to ask Rojas to resign. A plebiscite in December 1957 approved the National Front, under which the two parties would alternate in the presidency and share Congress equally. Alberto Lleras Camargo took office in August 1958.
KEN-1960: The Mau Mau insurgency had been militarily defeated by 1956, but the Emergency ran until January 1960. At the first Lancaster House conference in early 1960, the Colonial Secretary imposed a constitution that gave Africans a majority in the Legislative Council. Elections followed in 1961, and Britain handed over power at independence in December 1963. The colonial executive conceded an elected African majority before leaving.
KEN-1992: The Saba Saba riots of July 1990, demanding multiparty politics, were met with lethal repression. In November 1991, donors froze aid, and in December KANU and Parliament repealed Section 2A of the constitution, legalizing opposition parties. Daniel arap Moi won the multiparty elections of December 1992. The ruler kept power, but he now faced an elected opposition in parliament.
TUR-1961: On 27 May 1960, the military overthrew Adnan Menderes's Democrat Party government in an almost bloodless coup. The Constitution of 1961, approved by referendum in July, created a bicameral parliament, a constitutional court, and wider civil liberties. Elections were held in October 1961, and the military returned power to civilians. The new constitution was designed to constrain the executive far more than the one it replaced.
TTO-1962: The People's National Movement held mass rallies in 1959–60 and won the election of December 1961. After the Marlborough House conference of mid-1962, Trinidad and Tobago became independent on 31 August 1962 as a dominion on the Westminster model. The colonial executive was replaced by a cabinet responsible to an elected House of Representatives. Independence came by negotiation.
TZA-1962: TANU won the Legislative Council elections of 1958–59 and 1960, and Julius Nyerere became chief minister. Tanganyika became independent from Britain on 9 December 1961 and a republic with Nyerere as president one year later. The colonial governor was replaced by an elected government. Independence was negotiated without violence.
TZA-1990: In 1990–91, Nyerere publicly backed political pluralism, and President Mwinyi appointed the Nyalali Commission to consult the country. The Commission reported in December 1991, the ruling CCM accepted multiparty politics in February 1992, and parliament amended the constitution to end the party's monopoly. CCM remained in power and won the first multiparty elections in 1995. The ruler conceded competition from above.
BWA-1969: Bechuanaland became independent Botswana in September 1966, by negotiation with Britain, with Seretse Khama as president. Parliamentary government then bedded in. The first post-independence general election, in October 1969, was competitive and peaceful: the ruling BDP won 24 of 31 seats and three opposition parties the rest. The index records the consolidation of an elected legislature rather than a single reform.
PRT-1974: On 25 April 1974, the Armed Forces Movement toppled Caetano's Estado Novo in a nearly bloodless coup. Huge popular demonstrations followed, and the turbulent transition saw failed coups in March and November 1975. Elections to a Constituent Assembly were held in April 1975, the Constitution was adopted in 1976, and legislative and presidential elections followed. The index of legislative constraints rose from 0.03 in 1973 to 0.75 in 1974, and stabilized above 0.9 from 1976.
ESP-1977: Franco died in November 1975, and Juan Carlos I became king. Adolfo Suárez, appointed in July 1976, had the Francoist Cortes pass the Law for Political Reform, which voters approved by referendum in December 1976. Parties were legalized, and the first free elections since the 1930s were held on 15 June 1977. The Moncloa Pacts followed, and the Constitution of 1978 established a parliamentary monarchy.
BDI-1981: After the first UPRONA congress in December 1979, a party Central Committee replaced the military Supreme Revolutionary Council. A new constitution was approved by referendum in November 1981, and one-party elections to a National Assembly followed in October 1982, the first since 1965. President Bagaza stayed in power and was elected in 1984. The opening was limited to a legislature within a single party.
ZAF-1984: The Constitution of 1983, approved by white voters in a referendum, created a Tricameral Parliament with separate chambers for Whites, Coloureds and Indians, while still excluding the Black majority. The Tricameral Parliament opened on 3 September 1984, the same day the Vaal uprising began. The township revolt that followed led to a national state of emergency in 1986. The index records a partial concession by the ruling National Party, not the end of apartheid, which came in 1994.
TWN-1989: The Democratic Progressive Party was founded in September 1986 and tolerated by Chiang Ching-kuo. Martial law was lifted in July 1987, opposition parties were legalized in 1989, and the DPP contested the legislative elections of December 1989 openly. The National Affairs Conference of 1990 led to full elections for the legislature in 1991–92. The Kuomintang kept power throughout, conceding competition from above.
BEN-1990: Strikes by students, teachers and civil servants over unpaid wages ran through 1989. In December 1989, Mathieu Kérékou dropped Marxism-Leninism. The National Conference of February 1990 declared itself sovereign, named Nicéphore Soglo prime minister, and set up a transition. A new constitution was approved by referendum in December 1990, and Kérékou lost the presidential election of March 1991 to Soglo.
BGR-1990: On 10 November 1989, the Central Committee of the Communist Party removed Todor Zhivkov after 35 years in power, in an intra-party coup. Round Table talks in early 1990 produced free elections in June 1990, won by the renamed Socialist Party. A general strike forced the Lukanov government out in November 1990, and a new constitution followed in July 1991. The opposition took office after the elections of October 1991.
COG-1990: Under pressure from the trade unions, including a general strike in September 1990, the ruling PCT gave up Marxism-Leninism and agreed to multiparty politics. The Sovereign National Conference of 1991 stripped Denis Sassou Nguesso of most of his powers and installed a transitional prime minister. A new constitution was adopted by referendum in March 1992, and Pascal Lissouba defeated Sassou in the presidential election of August 1992.
CZE-1990: On 17 November 1989, riot police beat student demonstrators in Prague. Mass demonstrations and a general strike followed, and on 28–29 November the Communist Party gave up its leading role. Round-table talks led to Václav Havel's election as president in December 1989 and to free elections in June 1990. The Velvet Revolution ended communist rule without a single death.
HUN-1990: János Kádár was pushed out in May 1988. Large peaceful demonstrations followed, including the reburial of Imre Nagy in June 1989. The National Round Table of June–September 1989 negotiated the transition, the ruling party dissolved itself in October, and the Republic was proclaimed on 23 October 1989. Free elections in March–April 1990 put an opposition coalition in power.
MAR-1990: The general strike of December 1990 turned into riots in Fez and Tangier, which security forces put down. King Hassan II then liberalized from above: he created a human-rights council in 1990, released political prisoners in 1991, and held a constitutional referendum in September 1992 that enlarged the role of parliament. A further revision followed in 1996, and the opposition entered government in 1998. The King kept his throne and conceded constraints on his own power.
MNG-1990: Pro-democracy demonstrations began in December 1989, and a hunger strike in March 1990 forced the resignation of Batmönkh and the dissolution of the Politburo. The constitution was amended in the spring of 1990 to legalize opposition parties. The ruling MPRP won the multiparty elections of July 1990, and the Constitution of 1992 established a parliamentary democracy. Communist rule ended by concession, without violence.
NPL-1990: The Nepali Congress and the United Left Front launched the People's Movement in February 1990, with nationwide strikes and protests. Police fired on crowds in several cities. On 8 April 1990, King Birendra lifted the ban on political parties, and an interim government took office. The Constitution of November 1990 established a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament. The King kept his throne.
POL-1990: Strike waves in 1988 pushed the communist regime into talks with Solidarity. The Round Table of February–April 1989 agreed on semi-free elections, which Solidarity swept in June 1989. Tadeusz Mazowiecki's non-communist government took office in September 1989, the ruling party dissolved itself in January 1990, and Lech Wałęsa was elected president in December 1990. The transition was negotiated and peaceful.
ROU-1990: Protests began in Timișoara in December 1989 and spread to Bucharest. The army switched sides on 22 December, Nicolae Ceaușescu fled, and the National Salvation Front took power. Ceaușescu and his wife were executed on 25 December. Multiparty elections followed in May 1990, though the new government was shaken by the violent Mineriads of 1990 and 1991.
YEM-1990: North and South Yemen agreed on unification, proclaimed on 22 May 1990, under a power-sharing, multiparty transition. A constitution was approved by referendum in May 1991, and the first multiparty parliamentary elections were held in April 1993. The two former single-party regimes merged into a system with an elected legislature. The transition was marred by political assassinations, and civil war followed in 1994.
ALB-1991: Protests in Shkodër and Kavajë and the embassy crisis of 1990 were followed by student demonstrations in Tirana. In December 1990, the Party of Labour allowed political pluralism, and Hoxha's statue was toppled in February 1991. The communists won the elections of March 1991, but a general strike brought down the government in June and led to a coalition. The Democratic Party won the elections of March 1992, and Ramiz Alia resigned.
CPV-1991: In February 1990, the ruling PAICV held an emergency congress to end one-party rule, and the opposition MpD formed in April. The one-party state was abolished in September 1990. The MpD won the legislative elections of January 1991, and António Mascarenhas Monteiro won the presidency in February 1991. PAICV handed over power peacefully.
MLI-1992: Pro-democracy protests in Bamako peaked on 22 March 1991, when soldiers fired on demonstrators. After a general strike, Lieutenant Colonel Amadou Toumani Touré's coup ousted Moussa Traoré on 26 March 1991. A national conference met in August 1991, a constitutional referendum followed in January 1992, and Alpha Oumar Konaré won the presidential election of 1992. The military handed power to an elected government within a year.
GHA-1993: Under pressure from donors and the opposition, Jerry Rawlings's PNDC set a timetable for the return to civilian rule in March 1992. A constitutional referendum in April 1992 approved the Constitution of the Fourth Republic, the ban on parties was lifted in May, and Rawlings won the presidential election of November 1992. The opposition boycotted the parliamentary election, but the Fourth Republic began on 7 January 1993. The ruler kept power under a constitution that constrained him.
THA-1993: After the coup of February 1991, coup leader General Suchinda Kraprayoon became an unelected prime minister in April 1992. Mass protests in May 1992 were crushed by troops, with dozens killed. After the King's intervention, Suchinda resigned, and a constitutional amendment required the prime minister to be an elected member of parliament. The elections of September 1992 brought Chuan Leekpai's civilian government to power.
SLV-1994: The civil war between the government and the FMLN, which killed more than 75,000 people, ended with the UN-brokered Chapultepec Peace Accords of January 1992. The FMLN disarmed and became a legal party in December 1992. It took part in the elections of 1994, won by ARENA. The settlement reduced the army's political role and opened the legislature to the former insurgents.
IDN-1999: The Asian financial crisis of 1997–98 was followed by mass student protests. After security forces shot four students in May 1998, riots in Jakarta and other cities killed more than a thousand people. Suharto resigned on 21 May 1998, after 32 years in power, and handed over to Habibie. Free legislative elections followed in June 1999, the first since 1955, and constitutional amendments shifted power to the legislature.
NGA-1999: General Sani Abacha died suddenly in June 1998. His successor, General Abdulsalami Abubakar, released political prisoners and set a timetable for the transition. Elections ran from December 1998 to February 1999, the Constitution of 1999 was issued, and power passed to Olusegun Obasanjo on 29 May 1999. The military returned power to an elected president and National Assembly.
COM-2000: Anjouan and Mohéli declared secession in 1997, and a failed federal invasion of Anjouan left dozens dead. Colonel Azali took power in a bloodless coup in April 1999. The Fomboni Accords of February 2001 and a constitutional referendum in December 2001 created the federal Union of the Comoros, with an elected assembly and autonomy for the islands. Elections were held in 2002.
HRV-2000: President Franjo Tuđman died in December 1999. The opposition coalition led by the SDP and HSLS defeated the HDZ in the parliamentary elections of January 2000, and Stjepan Mesić won the presidency. Constitutional amendments in November 2000 moved Croatia from a semi-presidential to a parliamentary system. Power passed from the presidency to parliament by election.
SRB-2000: After the federal election of September 2000, the electoral commission refused to recognize Vojislav Koštunica's outright victory. A general strike and mass protests followed, and on 5 October 2000 hundreds of thousands stormed the federal parliament in Belgrade. Slobodan Milošević conceded the next day. The DOS coalition won the Serbian parliamentary election of December 2000.
SVK-2001: In the elections of September 1998, Vladimír Mečiar's HZDS won the most votes but could not form a government, and Mikuláš Dzurinda's coalition took office. Rudolf Schuster defeated Mečiar in the first direct presidential election in 1999. In February 2001, parliament passed a comprehensive constitutional amendment that strengthened judicial independence and other institutions as part of EU accession. The period of democratic backsliding ended by election.
IRQ-2003: The US-led invasion began in March 2003, and Baghdad fell on 9 April, ending Saddam Hussein's Ba'athist regime. The Coalition Provisional Authority ran the country until June 2004. Elections for a transitional National Assembly were held in January 2005, the permanent constitution was adopted by referendum in October 2005, and a full-term parliament was elected in December 2005. The elected legislature was created under occupation and amid insurgency.
BFA-2013: Mass protests and army mutinies in 2011 shook Blaise Compaoré's rule, and the index records a political opening in the years before his fall. In October 2014, protests against a constitutional amendment that would have extended his term led to the burning of parliament, and Compaoré resigned after 27 years in power. A short military interlude was followed by a civilian transition, and a coup by the presidential guard in September 2015 failed after popular resistance. Elections were held in November 2015.
